background.definition: Primary vulvar and vaginal malignancies comprise a heterogeneous group of tumors and include invasive [squamous cell carcinoma, melanoma, adenocarcinoma, Paget disease, sarcoma, basal cell carcinoma (BCC)] and preinvasive squamous cell lesions [VIN and vaginal intraepithelial neoplasia (VAIN)].

list.listitem: Vulvar carcinoma accounts for 3490 new cases and 880 deaths per year.
Vaginal cancer accounts for 2140 new cases and 790 deaths per year.
VIN has increased over fourfold in incidence between 1973 and 2000 (2.86 per 100,000 in 2000), whereas invasive carcinoma has increased only 20%.

VIN and VAIN are high-grade squamous lesions and are subdivided into usual-type VIN (including warty, basaloid, and mixed VIN) and differentiated VIN. Usual-type VIN is commonly associated with carcinogenic genotypes of human papillomavirus (HPV) and other HPV persistence risk factors, such as cigarette smoking and immunocompromised status. Differentiated VIN usually is not associated with HPV and is more often associated with vulvar dermatologic conditions, such as lichen sclerosis.
VIN and VAIN seem to be precursors for invasive vulvar and vaginal cancers, but invasive cancers are less well associated with HPV.
Vaginal clear cell adenocarcinoma is associated with in utero exposure to diethylstilbestrol (DES) and is most commonly diagnosed in young women.
VIN and VAIN are most often diagnosed in premenopausal women and are believed to be precursor lesions for squamous cell malignancies of the vulva and vagina.
VIN, VAIN, and squamous cell cancers tend to be multicentric (more than 1 lesion at presentation). More than 50% of woman with VIN and VAIN also have cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN).
Some cases of vulvar squamous cell cancers are associated with chronic vulvar dystrophies, such as lichen sclerosis, rather than HPV.
Extramammary Paget disease and vulvar BCC are associated with increased risk of other noncontiguous malignancies, such as those of breast, ovary, colon, and kidney.
Vaginal and vulvar malignancies are quite rare, so screening asymptomatic women is not cost effective. B
Women with a prior history of gynecologic malignancy should be screened with (at least) an annual pap smear and bimanual pelvic examination. C
Women with lichen sclerosis should probably have careful external examination, with or without a colposcope, at least once per year. C

The HPV vaccine ( Gardasil) may reduce the incidence of VIN, VAIN, and vaginal/vulvar squamous cell malignancies. A Danish registry study saw a decreasing incidence of vulvar high-grade precancerous lesions after introduction of the HPV vaccine in that county in women <20 and 20 to 29 years of age.C

The predominant high risk HPV type is HPV16, but other types HPV33 and HPV18 are also associated with vulvar cancer in a recent survey. Therefore, these types should be considered in developing vaccines.
Malignancy should be suspected when a vaginal or vulvar lesion does not respond to what is believed to be appropriate therapy. C
Diagnosis of vulvar and vaginal malignancies is often delayed because of absent or subtle symptoms. C
Diagnosis requires biopsy of suspicious lesion(s). C

list.listitem: Diagnosis is based on pathologic examination of tissue.

The most common presenting symptoms for VIN and vulvar cancer are a palpable lesion with or without bleeding and pruritis. Consider biopsy of all pigmented vulvar lesions and all condylomata in post-menopausal women.

The most common presenting symptoms for VAIN and vaginal cancer are abnormal discharge or vaginal bleeding. A high percentage of patients are asymptomatic at the time of diagnosis and are diagnosed by abnormal cytology.

A careful visual inspection of the external genitalia and vaginal wall (during the withdrawal of a speculum) is the most important tool in diagnosis. Cervical and vaginal pap smear should always be obtained. Careful palpation of the vulva, vaginal wall, pelvic structures, rectovaginal space, and groin nodes are also important. Colposcopic examination may be required.

In a clinic where women were referred for a suspicious vulvar lesion, 8.1% were diagnosed with vulvar cancer and 6.1% had a premalignant lesion. Of 140 women with irritation only and no visible lesion or bleeding, none had cancer.

The diagnosis is confirmed with biopsy of the lesion. Multiple biopsies should be taken if there are multiple lesions. Biopsy of the center of larger lesions is helpful for grading the tumor. Unlike biopsies of the cervix, vaginal and vulvar biopsies require local anesthetic.

After cleansing the epithelium with antiseptic, the area to be biopsied is infiltrated subcutaneously with 1% xylocaine with epinephrine. Once anesthesia is achieved, biopsies can be obtained with either a biopsy punch (such as Keyes) or cervical biopsy instrument (such as Tischler or Burke). Hemostasis is then obtained using Monsel solution, or the defect can be closed with absorbable suture (which is often more comfortable and quicker to heal).
Once the diagnosis of invasive malignancy is determined, the patient should be referred to gynecologic oncology for appropriate staging and treatment.
A systematic review of 10 studies found sensitivity of 70% and specificity of 90% (LR+ 3.5, LR- 0.22) for preoperative lympho node staging using 18F-FDG PET/CT.
Vaginal and vulvar malignancies are rare and often present with subtle or nonspecific symptoms and variable appearance (nodule, macule, ulcer, wart like).
Symptoms of concern include pruritis, nonhealing ulcer, abnormal vaginal discharge, and abnormal vaginal bleeding.
Diagnosis requires the clinician to proceed promptly to biopsy of any suspicious lesion(s).
Clinicians should consider performing a pap smear for diagnostic purposes in patients with vaginal and vulvar symptoms, when no visible lesion is present.
Treatment is directed by the stage of disease at diagnosis and usually requires lymph node dissection and extensive pelvic surgery. C

Treatment usually includes combinations of surgery, radiation, and chemotherapy, with more aggressive treatment for higher stage disease. Treatment is best carried out at specialized centers to reduce unnecesary morbidity. B
VIN and VAIN are treated with surgery, radiation, and 5-FU or imiquimod, with variable success rates and high rates of recurrence in small series.B
Quatravalent HPV vaccine (Gardisil) may reduce the risk of recurrent or future HPV related disease in women being treated for VIN and cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN). B

Preoperative chemotherapy with agents such as 5-FU, cisplatin, bleomycin, and mitomycin, with or without radiotherapy, has shown benefit for stage III and stage IV vulvar tumors. These chemotherapeutic agents, in combination with radiotherapy, have also been used in the treatment of stage II to stage IV vaginal carcinoma.
Topical 5-FU can be used for treatment of VIN and VAIN after careful evaluation to rule out invasive disease. Recurrence rates are similar to those with surgical treatments.

Topical imiquimod has been used for treatment of VIN after careful evaluation to rule out invasive disease. This is supported by a Cochrane review of 5 RCTs, which found a higher proportion of responders among those treated with topical imiquimod than placebo at 6 months (RR 11.9; 95% CI, 3.2-44) and 12 months (RR 9.1; 95% CI, 2.4-35).

A randomised trial of topical imiquimod versus surgical excision in high grade intraepithelial squamous lesions concluded that imiquimod was non-inferior with 80% clinical clinical response at follow-up. This supports the use of imiquimod as an effective, well accepted option for first line therapy in this group of patients.

Surgical therapy for invasive squamous cell cancers range from wide local excision for stage Ia to radical vulvectomy, bilateral lymph node dissection, and pelvic exenteration for stage III and stage IV disease.
A European expert consensus agreed that sentinel node biopsy should be undertaken at time of surgery for women with vulval malignancy to guide need for more radical lymph node dissection.

A survey of NCCN data in early stage vulval cancer demonstrated that only 66% of patients received lymph node evaluation concordant with guidelines. This was less likely in older patients, black patients and in low volume hospitals and was associated with worse outcomes.
Pre-operative staging with PET-CT if negative for groin nodes may spare the patients with early vulval cancer an unnecessary groin dissection if they are not suitable for sentinel node biopsy.
There have been limited clinical trials; a Cochrane review found that radical local excision appeared to be similarly effective to radical vulvectomy for women with early stage vulvar malignancy.
Sarcoma, melanoma, and Bartholin tumors are generally treated with wide local excision and lymph node dissection.
Vulvar Paget’s disease has traditionally been treated with wide local excision, but may have lower rates of recurrence if Mohs micrographic surgery is employed.
BCC and verrucous carcinoma are treated with only local excision.
Wide local excision or laser vaporization are used for the treatment of VIN and VaIN, after careful colposcopic examination and biopsies to rule out invasive disease.

European guidelines recommend follow-up for VaIN 1 (low grade vaginal squamous intraepithelial lesions), and active treatment for VaIN 2 or 3 (high grade vaginal squamous intraepithelial lesions). Surgery is recommended as the primary treatment option, with imiquimod for persistent multifocal lesions or for patients who are not surgical candidates. Tricholoaetic acid and 5-FU are not recommended.
Patients who undergo surgical treatment for vaginal and vulvar malignancies often suffer extensive changes in sexual function and identity. Behavioral therapy may be helpful.

Radiation therapy for squamous cell malignancies is most effective when combined with surgery and/or chemotherapy. A systematic review found, based on limited evidence, that while primary radiotherapy may cause less morbidity, recurrence and survival are not as good as for primary surgical therapy.

A 2017 survey of the National Cancer Database identified 1352 patients with squamous carcinoma of the vulva treated by radiotherapy. Five year survival was higher in patients who had chemoradiotherapy compared to radiotherapy alone (49.9% vs 27.4%).
Complications associated with radiation therapy make it inappropriate for preinvasive and stage I and stage II vulvar malignancies.
Stage I vaginal malignancies (less than 2 cm in size, without local extension) can be treated with intracavitary radiation therapy alone.
Stage II to stage IV vaginal malignancies are usually treated with a combination of radiotherapy (both external beam and intracavitary or interstitial) and surgery.

A systematic review found only limited quality studies of chemoradiation as a treatment for vulvar malignancy. A single RCT found no difference with neoadjuvant chemoradiation compared with primary surgery; 2 nonrandomized trials found no difference between primary chemoradiation and primary surgery, although most of the women who received chemoradiation did so because they were felt to be poor surgical candidates, creating a bias.
Once the diagnosis of VIN, VAIN, or invasive vaginal/vulvar malignancy is made, most patients should be referred to gynecologic oncology for definitive staging and treatment.
Five-year survival for vulvar cancer varies from 77% for stage I disease to 0% for stage IV disease. B
Five-year survival for vaginal cancer is 67% for stage I disease and 20% for stage IVa. B
Recurrence of squamous cell cancers is common because of the multicentric nature of the disease. B
VIN and VAIN are thought to be precursor lesions for invasive squamous carcinomas. All are rare enough that only small series are available. These predict progression rates of less than 50%.
Invasive cancers are thought to progress universally to death if left untreated.
Five-year survival rates for treated vulvar cancer are 77% for stage I disease, 54.8% for stage II, 30.8% for stage III, and 0% for stage IV disease (17% 3-year survival).
Five-year survival for treated vaginal cancer is 67% for stage I disease, 38.5% for stage II, 33.4% for stage III, and 20% for stage IVa (only 11% 3-year survival for stage IVb-distant mets).
Recurrence of VIN occurs in one-third of women, regardless of treatment employed. Progression to invasive squamous carcinoma occurs in 4% to 8% of women following treatment.
Small series show recurrence rates of 0% to 60% for VAIN treated with surgery, radiation, or topical 5-FU.

Women who have been treated for vulvar and vaginal malignancies (including intraepithelial neoplasias) require colposcopy, pap cytology, and pelvic examination at least every 6 months for 2 years and then yearly for life.
Because vulvar and vaginal malignancies are rare, there are no specific follow-up guidelines. Most experts recommend follow-up similar to that for cervical carcinoma.
Regular follow-up is important for discovery of recurrent disease and other cancers within the genital tract.
